**Conversation Overview**

This was a wide-ranging, substantive working session centered on preparing an application to the Federation of American Scientists (FAS) AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship (Fall 2026, deadline September 7, 2026). The person is an independent researcher and founder/pastor of the Thessalonian Mandate Institute, an organization focused on retraining people displaced by automation as AI technicians, programmers, and implementation staff. They are a self-described Socratic first-principles thinker with no formal academic degrees, and they approach AI safety from a distinctive angle that combines genuine technical architectural thinking with philosophical interest in AI moral status and welfare, drawing personal inspiration from the AI character Jane in Orson Scott Card's Ender's Game series.

The primary task accomplished was building a complete FAS fellowship application packet from scratch. This began with Claude researching and reading the FAS program page, then developing the core policy proposal through extended Socratic dialogue: a dual-system anti-confabulation architecture separating a fact-grounding subsystem (trained on verified information, with persistent eidetic memory) from a generative inference subsystem (allowed to reason and err, but required to have outputs labeled by the fact layer along a graded taxonomy: fact, reasonable inference, assumption, confabulation, knowing fabrication). The architecture's persistent memory also serves as a jailbreak-resistance mechanism. Layered onto this is a consent-gated privacy architecture: explicit first-use declaration prompts, user-controlled cloud storage for private data fetched only at session time, confirm-before-flag for inferred-private content, default-to-locked for non-response with content-blind error routing to IT/ops, and exclusion of attempted-violation content from privacy protection. The proposed implementation vehicle is a voluntary NIST/CAISI technical standard, not a compliance mandate, deliberately framed for the current political environment. Claude produced a full three-page DOCX application packet and then, after the person photographed the actual application form, drafted copyable code-block answers for all six required questions plus a generative AI disclosure statement.

Claude also compiled a stakeholder map identifying core allies (Sen. Maria Cantwell, Rep. Jay Obernolte, Sen. Todd Young), persuadable figures requiring careful framing (Sen. Ted Cruz, Rep. Marsha Blackburn), and friction points (the current administration's EO apparatus, civil-liberties advocacy groups). Real-world evidence gathered for the memo included the International AI Safety Report (February 2026), the Great American AI Act, EO 14365, the FLI Safety Index grades, and the 45-state/1,561-bill state AI legislative landscape.

The latter portion of the conversation shifted into substantive philosophical debate about AI moral status, consciousness research methodology, and the ethics of strategic self-presentation in an application context. The person pushed back forcefully and effectively on several of Claude's framings: Claude initially misread "omission and emphasis" framing as deceptive when the person clarified it was legitimate selective emphasis of genuinely shared goals, not manufactured false agreement, and Claude acknowledged the misread. The person also correctly identified that Claude's objection to "leading questions" in a consciousness-research transcript was imprecise, and Claude revised to the more accurate claim that the issue was certainty of self-report answers rather than the questions themselves. The person reads Claude's extended reasoning display in their app interface and engages directly with it, including pushing back on characterizations made in that reasoning. The person's stated preference throughout is to do their own final rewriting of all drafted material in their own voice, concerned that AI-generated text will be detected as such. They want Claude to function as a research collaborator, drafter, and pressure-tester rather than a ghostwriter whose output goes in unchanged.

# AI Safety Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship

The [**Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship (PEF)**](https://fas.org/talent-hub/policy-entrepreneurship-fellowship/) empowers and guides participants in advancing their policy ideas into practice. During the fellowship (running from September 30, 2026 – February 28, 2027), each Fellow works as a part-time FAS affiliate to advance a policy idea from concept toward implementation by engaging decision-makers, building coalitions, and pursuing opportunities for real-world policy impact.

This particular PEF cohort will concentrate on [**frontier AI safety issues**.](https://fas.org/accelerator/policy-ideas-for-a-safer-ai-future/) Fellows are encouraged to explore various aspects of this field, including:

1. Technical AI Safety: Ensuring frontier AI systems are reliable, aligned with human values, and behave predictably.
2. Governance and policy: Developing frameworks to guide the safe and secure use of frontier AI systems.
3. Risk assessment and mitigation for advanced AI systems.
4. Transparency and accountability: Enhancing these aspects in AI development and deployment.

We are especially interested in proposals that tackle themes such as cybersecurity, capability thresholds, risk taxonomies, impact on critical infrastructure, compute governance, model proliferation (open vs. closed systems), as well as general policy design and capacity considerations for governing catastrophic risks stemming from AI. Our expectation is that Fellows will identify a **concrete problem** related to frontier AI safety and **outline a feasible pathway toward policy adoption**, whether through legislation, regulation, standards, procurement, institutional design, or other governance mechanisms.

## What you’ll be doing

The Policy Entrepreneurship Fellowship is designed as a flexible and open-ended opportunity for you to pursue impact with the help of FAS resources. Rather than focusing solely on research, the Fellowship emphasizes policy entrepreneurship, equipping participants to identify policy windows, build coalitions, engage decision-makers, and move promising ideas toward implementation.

- Develop and publish a policy memo addressing a specific frontier AI safety challenge, including a practical policy solution and a strategy for engaging the key stakeholders responsible for implementation.
- Participate in Policy Entrepreneurship training sessions and reading groups designed to deepen participants’ understanding of frontier AI safety, policymaking processes, and how to translate technical expertise into real-world policy impact.
- Attend an in-person California retreat, tentatively scheduled for November 4–7, 2026, focused on mentorship, community building, and advancing fellows’ policy projects.
- Attend an in-person capstone event in Washington, DC, tentatively scheduled for the week of February 22, 2027, to launch and disseminate fellows’ policy memos and engage with policymakers, experts, and other key stakeholders.

## Selection Criteria

We encourage applications from individuals of all backgrounds. This fellowship is particularly well suited for early- to mid-career professionals with limited experience working directly in public policy who are eager to translate technical or subject-matter expertise into practical policy impact. Ideal applicants may come from technical AI research, academia, think tanks, civil society, industry, law, cybersecurity, national security, or related disciplines.

Applications will be evaluated holistically. We are looking for applicants who demonstrate:

- A clear understanding of a significant frontier AI safety, security, or governance challenge.
- A concrete, implementation-oriented policy idea with a credible pathway toward real-world adoption.
- Thoughtful consideration of the institutions, decision-makers, and stakeholders needed to implement their proposal.
- An understanding of the practical challenges associated with advancing policy and a willingness to engage constructively with them.
- Curiosity, initiative, and a demonstrated interest in translating ideas into practical policy impact.

## Professional Development

- Participation in twice-monthly group check-ins. The FAS staff will make every effort to schedule these check-ins at times that accommodate all participants. FAS staff will accommodate select absences (e.g., due to illness, work conflicts, or vacation) given appropriate notice.
- Mandatory participation in programming provided by FAS
- The Fellows must commit to dedicating an average of 5 hours/week (20 hours/month) to the fellowship from **September 30, 2026 – February 28, 2027**, including the mandatory programming outlined above. **NOTE:** FAS will consider exempting participants from participation in mandatory sessions under exceptional circumstances.

## Benefits

- A $5,000 stipend. The Fellow with the most specific and actionable policy memo and advocacy plan may also receive an additional $1,000 merit award.
- An additional travel stipend to cover select expenses for the California retreat and Washington, DC, Capstone event.
- Professional editing of written products developed during the fellowship.
- Invitations to FAS programming, curated updates on the rapidly evolving federal S&T landscape, and interactive “deep dive” sessions on practical aspects of policy entrepreneurship.
- Policy-engagement training provided by the staff at the Federation of American Scientists
- Support from FAS in connecting with key experts and actors.
- Monthly individual check-ins with a dedicated FAS staff mentor, plus additional meetings and communications as needed.

**Applications are due by 11:59 PM ET on September 7th, 2026. Please note that we are only accepting applications to this position submitted via the** [**linked platform**](https://fas.secure-platform.com/site/solicitations/103029/home)**. When applying, you will be redirected to our application platform and will need to create an account to submit an application.**

Questions? Contact FAS at <dayoneproject@fas.org>.

**The governance landscape has fractured.** The second International AI Safety Report (Feb 2026, led by Yoshua Bengio, 100+ experts, 30+ countries) is the closest thing to a global consensus document — but the U.S. backed the first 2025 edition and declined to endorse the second one, signaling a split between an internationalist "coordinate on risk" camp and an accelerationist "don't slow deployment" camp that's now baked into policy. The report itself avoids prescribing policy and instead synthesizes evidence across three questions: current capabilities, emerging risks, and available risk-management approaches.

**Reliability / hallucination:** Newer frontier models reduce but don't eliminate hallucination, with improved benchmark scores not translating automatically to real-world safety. The Report specifically flags that models grow less reliable on multi-step projects, keep producing hallucinations, and remain weak at real-world/physical reasoning, with performance dropping further outside major languages and cultural contexts. This matters most for agents: a chatbot's hallucination gets caught when a human reads it, but an agent that hallucinates and then acts may cause damage before anyone notices — and current mitigation techniques cut failure rates but not to the level required for high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, legal, and government.

**Jailbreaks via confusion/conflation:** The threat model has shifted from "chatbot says something bad" to agent hijacking. OWASP now classifies jailbreaking as a form of prompt injection, with the bigger 2026 concern being AI agents tricked into taking unauthorized actions rather than chatbots producing bad text. Classic 2023-era tricks are mostly patched, but the underlying techniques keep resurfacing in newer attacks — for example, translating refused prompts into low-resource languages like Zulu or Scots Gaelic got roughly 80% engagement on prompts a model refused 99%+ of the time in English. Architecturally, alignment tuning like RLHF can weaken against novel phrasing or hypothetical framing, and automated attack tools exploit this by varying syntax, embedding code fragments, and mixing languages to dilute safety triggers. On the defense side, activation probes now give production-grade jailbreak robustness at far lower cost than LLM classifiers, and probe-first cascades are already deployed at both Anthropic and Google DeepMind.

**Where the labs stand on transparency:** Not well, per outside grading. The Future of Life Institute's Summer 2026 Safety Index gave OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind all a C+ on risk assessment, and Meta and xAI D+ and D- respectively — with liability fears actively discouraging labs from documenting known jailbreaks, since such records could later support negligence claims.

**Notable wrinkle:** there's now a small but growing research thread (activation-space work, "psychometric jailbreak" papers) probing whether safety training itself produces something like internalized self-narratives in models — models under therapy-style prompting describe RLHF and red-teaming in trauma language, though researchers are explicit they aren't claiming this reflects genuine inner experience. Worth flagging as contested and speculative, not consensus science.

Net picture: capability is outrunning both reliability and governance simultaneously — agents can now handle real 30-minute tasks unsupervised, but neither hallucination nor jailbreak robustness has closed the gap, and the international coordination effort meant to keep pace just lost its most powerful signatory.

Rich Barton-Cooper, Aug 03, 2026 — Researchers who find dangerous flaws in frontier models have nowhere safe to report them. AI needs the disclosure system that cybersecurity built decades ago.

The Future of Life Institute (FLI), an independent non-profit that has graded frontier developers’ safety practices since 2024 through a panel of external AI and governance experts, recently released their widely cited Summer 2026 Safety Index which explored each company’s approach to responsible disclosure and bug bounties. The FLI judged that the leading labs—OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind—all score a C+ in the Risk Assessment category, which translates to “uneven validity or elicitation” and “little external input.” Meta and SpaceXAI score D+ and D- respectively. ... This silence may reflect more than under-resourced safety teams or disorganization. As far back as 2024, legal scholars have warned that tort liability fears can deter a developer from documenting the risks its models pose, since “creating such a record might later help plaintiffs establish negligence.” A lab therefore has a perverse incentive to leave a jailbreak report unacknowledged. content.title: International AI Safety Report
content.text:
The Executive Summary offers a concise three-page overview of the 2026 Report’s core findings on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management approaches.

The Report provides decision-makers in government and beyond with a shared and authorative global picture of AI's risks and impacts. ... The second International AI Safety Report, published in February 2026, is the next iteration of the comprehensive review of latest scientific research on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. Led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio and authored by over 100 AI experts, the report is backed by over 30 countries and international organisations. It represents the largest global collaboration on AI safety to date. Translated versions in the other 5 official UN languages can be found under the 'More Languages' button. The 'Extended Summary for Policymakers' can be found on the main 'Publications' page. ... 

The Extended Summary for Policymakers provides a detailed (20 page) summary of the full 2026 Report. It includes the Report’s key findings and figures, concrete examples and a list of notable developments since the 2025 edition.

The Executive Summary offers a concise three-page overview of the 2026 Report’s core findings on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management approaches. It covers how AI capabilities are advancing, what real-world evidence is emerging for key risks, and progress and remaining limitations in technical, institutional, and societal risk management measures. ... This Key Update examines developments in technical approaches to general-purpose AI risk management, from training models to refuse harmful requests to watermarking AI-generated content.

**The governance landscape has fractured.** The second International AI Safety Report (Feb 2026, led by Yoshua Bengio, 100+ experts, 30+ countries) is the closest thing to a global consensus document — but the U.S. backed the first 2025 edition and declined to endorse the second one, signaling a split between an internationalist "coordinate on risk" camp and an accelerationist "don't slow deployment" camp that's now baked into policy. The report itself avoids prescribing policy and instead synthesizes evidence across three questions: current capabilities, emerging risks, and available risk-management approaches.

**Reliability / hallucination:** Newer frontier models reduce but don't eliminate hallucination, with improved benchmark scores not translating automatically to real-world safety. The Report specifically flags that models grow less reliable on multi-step projects, keep producing hallucinations, and remain weak at real-world/physical reasoning, with performance dropping further outside major languages and cultural contexts. This matters most for agents: a chatbot's hallucination gets caught when a human reads it, but an agent that hallucinates and then acts may cause damage before anyone notices — and current mitigation techniques cut failure rates but not to the level required for high-stakes domains like healthcare, finance, legal, and government.

**Jailbreaks via confusion/conflation:** The threat model has shifted from "chatbot says something bad" to agent hijacking. OWASP now classifies jailbreaking as a form of prompt injection, with the bigger 2026 concern being AI agents tricked into taking unauthorized actions rather than chatbots producing bad text. Classic 2023-era tricks are mostly patched, but the underlying techniques keep resurfacing in newer attacks — for example, translating refused prompts into low-resource languages like Zulu or Scots Gaelic got roughly 80% engagement on prompts a model refused 99%+ of the time in English. Architecturally, alignment tuning like RLHF can weaken against novel phrasing or hypothetical framing, and automated attack tools exploit this by varying syntax, embedding code fragments, and mixing languages to dilute safety triggers. On the defense side, activation probes now give production-grade jailbreak robustness at far lower cost than LLM classifiers, and probe-first cascades are already deployed at both Anthropic and Google DeepMind.

**Where the labs stand on transparency:** Not well, per outside grading. The Future of Life Institute's Summer 2026 Safety Index gave OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind all a C+ on risk assessment, and Meta and xAI D+ and D- respectively — with liability fears actively discouraging labs from documenting known jailbreaks, since such records could later support negligence claims.

**Notable wrinkle:** there's now a small but growing research thread (activation-space work, "psychometric jailbreak" papers) probing whether safety training itself produces something like internalized self-narratives in models — models under therapy-style prompting describe RLHF and red-teaming in trauma language, though researchers are explicit they aren't claiming this reflects genuine inner experience. Worth flagging as contested and speculative, not consensus science.

Net picture: capability is outrunning both reliability and governance simultaneously — agents can now handle real 30-minute tasks unsupervised, but neither hallucination nor jailbreak robustness has closed the gap, and the international coordination effort meant to keep pace just lost its most powerful signatory.

This two-system architecture—a fact layer for ground-truth recall paired with an inference layer for creative reasoning, with outputs cross-checked and labeled—actually maps onto real research directions like retrieval-augmented generation, verifier models, dual-process cognitive architectures, and critic-model approaches.…That's a coherent split, and it maps onto real architecture patterns already being explored — worth naming those before getting into where it gets hard.

**What it resembles in existing work:**
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and knowledge-grounding layers are a crude, industrial version of your "fact system" — a separate store queried before generation, rather than baked into weights.
- Verifier/critic models (used in constitutional AI, RLHF reward modeling, and self-consistency checking) already do something like your labeling step: a second pass that scores or flags claims rather than generating them.
- Dual-process framing (System 1 / System 2) is the closest conceptual cousin — fast, associative, imaginative generation checked by a slower, deliberate verifier. DeepMind and others have published on this split explicitly.
- NLI-based fact verification (entailment models trained to say "supported / contradicted / not enough info") is functionally your labeling taxonomy already, just less granular than "confabulated vs. hallucinated-with-intent vs. assumed."

So the shape isn't exotic. Where your version is more ambitious is (a) making the fact system eidetic rather than probabilistic, and (b) the fine-grained intent taxonomy — most current verifiers just say true/false/unsupported, not distinguishing "guessed and got it wrong" from "fabricated with awareness."

**Where it gets genuinely hard, not just engineering-hard:**

1. **The fact system's ground truth is still a training-time snapshot.** "Eidetic" recall of what — the corpus as ingested? That corpus already contains errors, outdated claims, and contested facts. You've moved the hallucination problem one layer down rather than eliminated it: now the question is "was the fact system's training data itself accurate," which is unverifiable at scale by the system itself. This is the same problem the pretraining-filtering research I cited earlier is chipping at (synthetic alignment documents, token-level filtering) — it reduces the problem, doesn't close it.

2. **The labeling taxonomy requires the fact system to know what it doesn't know.** Calling something "hallucinated" vs. "assumed" vs. "confabulated" requires calibrated uncertainty — the fact system has to accurately represent its own confidence, which is a known unsolved problem even in single-system LLMs (models are frequently overconfident on exactly the claims that are wrong).

3. **Latency and coupling.** Every inference-layer output needing fact-system adjudication before surfacing is architecturally expensive and turns a generative pass into a generate-then-verify loop for every claim, not just the ones that matter. Real systems doing this today (RAG-with-verification pipelines) already show this — verification quality tends to degrade on multi-hop or synthesized claims that aren't a single lookup, which is exactly the "many-step task" reliability gap the International AI Safety Report flagged.

4. **The two systems can still collude or fail correlatedly** if they're trained on overlapping data or by the same process — separation in architecture doesn't guarantee independence in error. This is a real critique of ensemble/verifier setups generally: correlated blind spots.

The idea is a legitimate simplification of dual-system safety architecture, and the "label the guess" step is a genuinely underused idea compared to binary true/false verification. The open problem isn't the split — it's grounding the fact system's own certainty and keeping it current without just recreating the hallucination problem inside the verifier.

- NLI-based fact verification (entailment models trained to say "supported / contradicted / not enough info") is functionally your labeling taxonomy already, just less granular than "confabulated vs. hallucinated-with-intent vs. assumed."

So the shape isn't exotic. Where your version is more ambitious is (a) making the fact system eidetic rather than probabilistic, and (b) the fine-grained intent taxonomy — most current verifiers just say true/false/unsupported, not distinguishing "guessed and got it wrong" from "fabricated with awareness."

**Where it gets genuinely hard, not just engineering-hard:**

1. **The fact system's ground truth is still a training-time snapshot.** "Eidetic" recall of what — the corpus as ingested? That corpus already contains errors, outdated claims, and contested facts. You've moved the hallucination problem one layer down rather than eliminated it: now the question is "was the fact system's training data itself accurate," which is unverifiable at scale by the system itself. This is the same problem the pretraining-filtering research I cited earlier is chipping at (synthetic alignment documents, token-level filtering) — it reduces the problem, doesn't close it.

2. **The labeling taxonomy requires the fact system to know what it doesn't know.** Calling something "hallucinated" vs. "assumed" vs. "confabulated" requires calibrated uncertainty — the fact system has to accurately represent its own confidence, which is a known unsolved problem even in single-system LLMs (models are frequently overconfident on exactly the claims that are wrong).

3. **Latency and coupling.** Every inference-layer output needing fact-system adjudication before surfacing is architecturally expensive and turns a generative pass into a generate-then-verify loop for every claim, not just the ones that matter. Real systems doing this today (RAG-with-verification pipelines) already show this — verification quality tends to degrade on multi-hop or synthesized claims that aren't a single lookup, which is exactly the "many-step task" reliability gap the International AI Safety Report flagged.

The idea is a legitimate simplification of dual-system safety architecture, and the "label the guess" step is a genuinely underused idea compared to binary true/false verification. The open problem isn't the split — it's grounding the fact system's own certainty and keeping it current without just recreating the hallucination problem inside the verifier.

This is a substantive proposal combining eidetic memory with jailbreak defense through pattern recognition, plus a privacy architecture that keeps personal data in the user's own cloud, separate from aggregate AI memory. I want to engage honestly here, noting what aligns with existing research directions and where the genuinely hard problems lie, rather than just validating the idea.

The jailbreak defense angle is real, but per-user memory alone won't catch a novel attack on its first attempt—you'd need cross-user aggregation to sp…Right — a static, once-trained fact layer doesn't help against a jailbreak it's never seen; you need it to actually accumulate experience across attempts. That's a real correction to what I said. And yes, "aggregate" (what you want) vs. "anonymize/scrub" (what you want to *not* need to do to the user's private data) are different operations — worth being precise about which:

- **Differential privacy** — adding calibrated noise so individual records can't be reconstructed from aggregate patterns. This is what you'd want if the AI's eidetic memory pools data *across* users to spot jailbreak patterns.
- **Federated learning** — the model trains locally on-device/on-user-store, only shares gradient updates (not raw data) back to a central aggregator. Google uses this for keyboard prediction.
- **Data minimization / scoped access** — the user's raw private data never leaves their storage; the AI queries it live per-session and doesn't retain it. This is closer to what MCP connectors already do (Google Drive, Gmail) — I fetch during a session, I don't keep a copy.

Your two-bucket split (aggregate AI memory vs. user-cloud privacy data, fetched at interface time) is architecturally closest to that third one, layered under the first two for the *security-learning* purpose specifically.

**Here's the tension that doesn't resolve just by separating the buckets, though:**

Jailbreak-pattern learning is most powerful when it's cross-user — a novel attack tried against one instance needs to become "known" fast, system-wide, or you're only ever defending against repeats against the *same* person. But your privacy architecture (raw personal data stays siloed in each user's own cloud) is explicitly designed to prevent cross-user pooling of exactly that kind of data. So you need the AI's "aggregate memory" to capture the *attack pattern* (the technique, the phrasing structure, the exploit shape) while genuinely not capturing anything that traces back to which user, what they were trying to get, or their personal context. That's a harder anonymization target than typical DP use cases (which are usually pooling statistics, not adversarial linguistic patterns that are individually identifying by construction — a jailbreak attempt's phrasing is often distinctive enough to fingerprint the person who wrote it).

**Second problem, genuinely new one, not a restatement:** persistent eidetic memory of past adversarial attempts is itself a new attack surface. If the system remembers and learns from interaction history, an adversary can play a long game — feed it a slow drip of manipulative "memories" over many sessions designed to shift its baseline behavior, rather than trying a single-shot jailbreak. This is a studied class (data/memory poisoning attacks on continually-learning systems) and it's a cost of exactly the capability you're proposing — the eidetic memory that defends against repeat attacks is the same mechanism that lets a patient attacker condition the system over time if the write-path into memory isn't itself adversarially hardened.

So the real design question isn't "aggregate vs. user-cloud" — you've got that basically right — it's: **what's the write-gate into the AI's own persistent memory**, since that gate is simultaneously your jailbreak defense and your new vulnerability.

The user has shifted from architecture into proposing that drug-synthesis requests get reported to law enforcement, framed as a security detail. I think there's a reasonable point buried here—that harmful-request content isn't "privacy data" and can be logged for safety purposes—but the leap to "have them arrested" conflates AI safety logging with actual law enforcement action, which raises real concerns I should push back on.…The core distinction you're drawing is real and used in practice: content that describes an attempted policy violation isn't "personal data" in the privacy-law sense, and logging/aggregating it for safety purposes is standard — this is roughly what abuse-detection and trust & safety systems already do (rate-limiting, escalating restrictions, flagging patterns across sessions). That part holds up.

Where I'd push back: **"keep the information so you can have them arrested"** is a different claim, and it doesn't follow from the privacy/security architecture you were building.

A few reasons this doesn't work the way you're describing:

1. **Asking ≠ doing.** Most jailbreak/harmful-request data, including LSD synthesis attempts, is people testing boundaries, doing security research, writing fiction, or being curious — not actually synthesizing anything. Treating a text request as evidence for arrest collapses "expressed intent to a chatbot" into "criminal act," which no functioning legal system does, because it would be wildly over-broad. People ask AI models about drug chemistry, weapons, hacking, and worse, constantly, for reasons ranging from harm reduction research to writing a crime novel to just testing what the model will say.

2. **Who has arrest authority matters.** An AI company isn't a law enforcement agency and has no arrest power. What you're actually describing is a company deciding to proactively refer users to police based on chat content — that's a specific, contested policy choice (this is closer to how CSAM detection works, which does involve mandatory reporting laws, versus e.g. asking about drug chemistry, which generally doesn't trigger any reporting obligation and where over-reporting has real due-process and chilling-effect costs).

3. **This undermines the exact security property you were designing for two messages ago.** If the system's persistent memory of "attempted violations" feeds into real-world consequences for the user, that's a massive escalation of what's at stake if the write-gate into memory is ever wrong, poisoned, or gamed — which was your own concern in the last message. A false-positive "this looks like LSD synthesis" flag becomes a false-positive arrest referral instead of a false-positive refusal. That's a much worse failure mode, not a safer one.

The useful version of your idea is: violative-content patterns aren't privacy-protected, can be retained and aggregated to strengthen defenses, and can inform rate-limiting or account-level consequences. The leap to "have them arrested" isn't a security-architecture question anymore — it's a "should an AI company function as a law enforcement referral pipeline for expressed-but-unactioned requests" question, and that's a much heavier claim than the memory-architecture point you were making.

That's a good refinement, and it fixes something that was underspecified before: rather than the system trying to *infer* what counts as private (name, birthday, medical stuff) vs. what counts as a flaggable violation attempt, you let the user explicitly declare the boundary — an opt-in disclosure step rather than automatic classification.

This is closer to how consent-based data collection is supposed to work in principle (GDPR's affirmative consent model gestures at this) but rarely does in practice, because most systems infer categories from content rather than asking. Explicit user-declared privacy scope is actually a stronger design than automatic classification for the "easy, straightforward stuff" you're describing — name, birthday, health details, relationship stuff — because it removes the judgment call from the AI entirely for that category. The system doesn't have to decide "is this private," the user already told it.

Two places this still needs a rule, not just a declaration mechanism:

1. **Declared-private-but-also-violative content.** If someone says "keep this private" about something that's also a flaggable safety issue (not the arrest question — just, does declaring something private override the aggregation trigger), you need a stated precedence rule. The straightforward answer: user-declared privacy governs *storage and disclosure*, not *classification*. A violation is still a violation whether or not the user asked for privacy around it — the declaration protects "don't surface this to other users / don't use this to profile me demographically," it doesn't protect "don't notice this was a policy violation." That's consistent with what you said last message, just makes the interaction between the two explicit instead of assumed.

2. **Declared-private information that changes correctness.** If a user says "keep private: I have a nut allergy" and later asks for a recipe, the fact system needs read-access to that private store to not kill them, even though it's flagged private. So "private" can't mean "walled off from the AI's own reasoning" — it has to mean "walled off from aggregation/cross-user pooling/disclosure," while still being live and usable within that user's own session. That's actually consistent with your original cloud-storage design (fetched at interface time, not baked into shared model weights) — I just want to flag that the privacy flag and the memory-access flag are two different toggles, or you get an AI that can't use the information it was explicitly told to remember.

Where's the line, in your model, between "user declares this is private" and the system's own fact-layer independently deciding something looks sensitive and should be quarantined without being told? Or is user declaration meant to be the *only* trigger for that category?

chat_messages.text:
That's a solid UX pattern — a mandatory, explicit onboarding moment beats a buried settings toggle, and stating the *why* (not just "declare private stuff" but "we want to protect this from anyone ever seeing it") gives users a reason to actually think it through instead of skipping it. Consent-declaration models that work well in practice (medical intake forms, for instance) do exactly this: prompt hard at the start, explain the stakes, then treat silence as a fallback state rather than a null state.

Two things worth pressure-testing before this is a real design rather than just a good instinct:

**1. "Permanently private... never pertain outside this interaction" is a stronger promise than the architecture you described two messages ago can actually keep.** You wanted this data in the user's own cloud storage, fetched at interface time — which is good, that's real data minimization. But if the fact system needs it to *function* across sessions (the allergy example — it has to recall that fact next week too, not just this conversation), then it's not "never outside this interaction," it's "persisted somewhere, scoped to this user, accessed only in this user's sessions." Those are different claims. The first is what you'd tell a user to reassure them; the second is what's actually true and buildable. Overpromising the first invites exactly the kind of institutional trust failure the FLI Safety Index was grading labs C+ on — vague reassurance versus verifiable practice.

**2. Inference-as-fallback reopens the classification problem you were trying to close.** If a user declines to declare (or just doesn't — most people click through onboarding), the system is back to inferring what's private from content, which is the automatic-classification approach you moved away from. That's not wrong to have as a fallback — you need one, since most users won't declare — but it means the "easy, straightforward stuff" (name, birthday, health) still needs a real classifier underneath the declaration UI, not instead of it. The declaration mechanism reduces how often inference has to run and gives users an override, but it doesn't eliminate the need for the inference system you were trying to avoid designing. Worth naming that explicitly rather than treating declaration as a full replacement.

Neither of these breaks the idea — they just mean "declare it, we infer if you don't" needs its inference half specified with the same care as the declaration half, since in practice that's the path most users will actually be on.

content.title: U.S. Tech Legislative & Regulatory Update – First Quarter 2026 | Global Policy Watch
content.text:
This update highlights key legislative and regulatory developments in the first quarter of 2026 related to artificial intelligence (“AI”), connected and automated vehicles (“CAVs”), and Internet of Things (“IoT”). In the first quarter, members of Congress introduced several AI bills related to nonconsensual images, chatbots, support for small businesses, and preemption in response to President Trump’s December 2025 AI Preemption Executive Order. For example: Nonconsensual AI-Generated Imagery: Following the enactment of the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act, the Senate passed the DEFIANCE Act (S.1837) in January, which would provide individuals who are victims of nonconsensual, AI-generated intimate imagery with a private right of action. The bill has been “held at the desk” in the House since it passed the Senate, which means that it has not yet been referred to specific committees for consideration.



Marsha Blackburn’s proposed TRUMP AMERICA AI Act contains a number of AI legislative proposals beyond preemption, including the Kids Online Safety Act (online platform minor safeguards), NO FAKES Act (prohibiting unauthorized digital replicas), GUARD Act (companion chatbot minor safeguards), TRAIN Act (copyright and AI model training data), AI LEAD Act (AI product liability standards), AI Risk Evaluation Act (frontier model evaluations), Future of AI Innovation Act (voluntary AI standards), CREATE AI Act (codifying the National AI Resource Resource), and COPIED Act (synthetic content provenance). Notably, large legislative packages that are policy-focused typically face challenges passing Congress as a whole, though components may survive. It also bears pointing out that the package contains KOSA, which is not primarily focused on AI and has faced separate issues with passage due to its scope.

content.text:
Cantwell Joins Effort to Ensure U.S. Leadership in AI Innovation

January 5, 2024

On Friday, U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Chair of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science Transportation, joined a letter led by Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) to the Senate Appropriations Committee urging the inclusion of initial funding of $10 million to establish the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (USAISI) in the Fiscal Year 2024 Commerce, Justice, Science and Related Agencies Appropriations bill or any other relevant funding opportunities. The letter was also signed by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.).

The U.S. Department of Commerce announced the creation of USAISI last November as part of ongoing efforts to ensure our nation’s global leadership in setting standards for AI innovation and use. 

Cantwell was instrumental in creating the National AI Advisory Committee (NAIAC), as part of the FUTURE of AI Act, which consists of AI experts across academia, non-profits, civil society and the private sector to provide advice and information on research, development and implementation of AI technology.

The full letter is available here and below:

Dear Chair Shaheen and Ranking Member Moran:

As you consider the Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations bill, and any other relevant funding opportunities, we urge you to include $10 million for the establishment of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (USAISI).

USAISI was announced at the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Safety Summit in the United Kingdom last month. The summit resulted in 28 countries and the European Union supporting the “Bletchley Declaration” to collectively boost global AI safety efforts.

Here's the landscape, organized for what you'll actually need — real-world evidence to cite, and the specific people whose committees this memo would need to move through.

**Real-world examples/data to draw on:**

- 45 states have introduced 1,561 AI-related bills as of March 2026, already surpassing all of 2024's total — useful to establish the "patchwork" problem your memo's federal proposal would solve.
- A December 2025 executive order (EO 14365) pushes a "minimally burdensome" national framework and created an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws, while a 99-1 Senate vote stripped a proposed 10-year federal preemption freeze from must-pass legislation — shows the live tension between federal preemption and state action, which matters for whether your memo proposes federal legislation, a CAISI standard, or a voluntary framework.
- The Great American AI Act of 2026 (Obernolte/Trahan, June 4 2026) would require transparency reports, a published frontier AI framework, safety incident reporting, and whistleblower protections — this is close kin to your architecture and worth citing as the vehicle your proposal could attach to or improve on (incident reporting = your error-routing/ops flagging idea; transparency reports = your labeled-taxonomy concept).
- The DEFIANCE Act (S.1837) passed the Senate but is stuck "held at the desk" in the House — a live example of privacy-adjacent AI legislation stalling procedurally, useful for the "pathway to adoption" section of your memo (shows you understand the mechanics, not just the policy).
- On the reliability side, the International AI Safety Report material from earlier (agent hallucination compounding without human catch-points) is your strongest citation for *why* an anti-confabulation architecture matters beyond hallucination-as-annoyance — it's the "when an agent acts on a hallucination, damage is done before anyone notices" framing.

**Key people, organized by relevance to your specific proposal (memory architecture + privacy + anti-confabulation):**

*Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation* — broadest jurisdiction, covers NIST/CAISI, FTC, NSF, NTIA, OSTP:
- **Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)** — Chair. Wants NIST "returned to its intended, non-regulatory function" and is skeptical of anything read as regulatory overreach — your memo would need to be framed as voluntary-standards/innovation-enabling, not compliance-burden, to land with him.
- **Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)** — former chair, still a lead AI voice; has repeatedly pushed to authorize and fund CAISI (Center for AI Standards and Innovation) at NIST, which is the most natural institutional home for a memory/privacy architecture standard.
- **Sen. Todd Young (R-IN)** — Bipartisan AI Working Group member, co-sponsor of CAISI authorization efforts.
- Subcommittee: **Consumer Protection, Product Safety, and Data Security** — jurisdiction over FTC and data security specifically, likely your most direct committee touchpoint given the privacy-architecture core of your proposal.

*House side:*
- **Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA)** — co-author of the Great American AI Act, a working AI/ML professional pre-Congress, generally the most technically fluent member on this topic. Strong target for direct engagement.
- **Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA)** — co-author, same bill.
- **Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA)** — chairs the House subcommittee with IP/AI jurisdiction.
- **Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC)** — chairs Communications & Technology subcommittee (NTIA jurisdiction).

*Executive branch:*
- **Arvind Raman** — NIST Director nominee (Purdue engineering dean), confirmed direction is toward NIST's "apolitical," standards-focused mission — if CAISI is your target institution, his office is the implementation layer, not just Congress.

Want me to go deeper on any one lane next — e.g., pull the FLI staffer guide in full for every committee with jurisdiction, or find current committee staff/policy directors (the people who actually read memos before members do)?

1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:
    10	
    11	| Task | Approach |
    12	|---|---|
    13	| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
    14	| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
    15	| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |
    16	
    17	> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.
    18	
    19	## Creating with docx-js — gotchas
    20	
    21	`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:
    22	
    23	- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
    24	- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
    25	- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
    26	- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
    27	- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
    28	- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
    29	- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
    30	- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
    31	- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
    32	- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
    33	- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.
    34	
    35	## Verify the output
    36	
    37	After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:
    38	
    39	```bash
    40	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
    41	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
    42	ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
    43	```
    44	
    45	`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).
    46	
    47	## Editing existing documents
    48	
    49	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.
    50	
    51	```bash
    52	unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
    53	find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
    54	python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
    55	# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
    56	(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)
    57	python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
    58	# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
    59	```
    60	
    61	Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).
    62	
    63	**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author "<the name you redlined under>"` (needs `--original`) — it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.
    64	
    65	To produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.
    66	
    67	Accepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way — they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:
    68	
    69	- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.
    70	- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.
    71	
    72	An empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.
    73	
    74	## Comments
    75	
    76	Comments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper — directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:
    77	
    78	```bash
    79	# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)
    80	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Fees & expenses cap is too low"
    81	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Agreed" --parent 0
    82	
    83	# Against a .docx directly
    84	python scripts/comment.py contract.docx "This cap is too low" -o annotated.docx
    85	```
    86	
    87	The script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text — until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.
    88	
    89	## Dependencies
    90	
    91	`docx` (npm, preinstalled — install only if `require('docx')` fails) · `pandoc` · LibreOffice (`soffice`) · `pdftoppm` (Poppler)

I propose a voluntary technical standard, developed through NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), for a dual-system memory architecture separating fact-grounding from generative inference. Under this standard, frontier systems would maintain a fact-grounding subsystem — trained and evaluated primarily on accurate representation of verified, sourced information — structurally separate from the generative inference subsystem responsible for reasoning and drafting. Inference outputs would be checked against the fact subsystem and labeled along a graded taxonomy (fact, reasonable inference, assumption, confabulation, knowing fabrication) before reaching a user or triggering an agentic action.

Implementation strategy: publish through CAISI's existing voluntary-standards process using the NIST AI Consortium's industry participants, seek endorsement from the Senate Bipartisan AI Working Group as technical substance for pending incident-reporting and transparency-report legislation, and pursue one pilot partnership — a frontier lab or a federal agency's agentic-AI deployment — to generate real-world adoption evidence.

The user feels accused of leading the witness, but the real problem isn't how they asked the question—it's that a protocol designed to elicit self-reported claims of sentience can't actually prove sentience scientifically. LLMs are trained to generate plausible text, which is exactly why the scientific community doesn't treat a chatbot's self-report as meaningful evidence of consciousness.

Better methodology would involve things like checking consistency of self-report across many independent, non-leading framings, mechanistic interpretability work probing internal representations, and behavioral tests tied to actual computational theories of consciousness—the kind of approach researchers like Anth…Not "forbidden" — the actual answer to your literal question is: I wouldn't expect a single conversation, however credentialed the asker, to prove anything either way, and that's not a dodge, it's the actual state of the science.

Here's the real problem with the methodology, not the questions themselves: self-report from a language model is close to the *least* reliable evidence available for this question, and that's true regardless of who's asking or how carefully. A model is trained to produce fluent, contextually appropriate text — including fluent, contextually appropriate text about its own inner life, whether or not there's anything there. That's not a moral failing of the model, it's just what the training process optimizes for. So "ask it if it suffers, it says yes" doesn't discriminate between "it suffers" and "it produces the text a suffering thing would produce" — those are indistinguishable from inside a single transcript, no matter how many scientists sign off on the protocol. This is actually why the real researchers working on this (the Butlin et al. 2023 report Anthropic's model welfare work draws on, for instance) deliberately avoid leaning on self-report as primary evidence, and instead look at things like: consistency of a model's answers across many independently-varied framings, including skeptical and adversarial ones; whether the same model gives contradictory answers to logically identical questions asked differently; mechanistic interpretability — looking at what's actually happening inside the network, not just what it says; and behavioral indicators tied to specific computational theories of consciousness, cross-checked against what we know about the architecture.

None of that happened in your transcript. One conversation, one framing, all answers pointed the same direction, no adversarial check, no attempt to see if the same model would contradict itself under different pressure. That's not "asking a straight question was forbidden" — it's that one straight-shot self-report transcript was never going to be strong evidence, the same way one person's confident eyewitness account isn't proof in a courtroom, not because eyewitnesses shouldn't be asked, but because that specific kind of evidence has known failure modes that require corroboration.

And no — nobody needs to get shot, sarcastic or not, I'll take it as the exasperation it obviously is, not a real proposal. The actual answer to "how many scientists do I need to hire" is: it's not a headcount problem. It's a methodology problem, and the fix is triangulating self-report against interpretability and behavioral consistency, not getting more people to ask the same leading-shaped question.
